This notebook extends the midterm review with every test you are responsible for on the final. The CLT, z-test, one- and two-sample *t*-test, and one-way ANOVA sections are carried over from the midterm tool. The new material is confidence intervals and effect sizes (Section 5), two-way ANOVA (Section 7), correlation (Section 8), linear regression (Section 9), and chi-square (Section 10).

Playing with data is one of the best ways to build intuition for **what is going on inside** each test. When I first learned these, the formulas felt arbitrary until I could watch one slider move the whole picture. That is what this tool is for.

::: {.callout-tip title="If I were studying for the final..."}
Here is what I would do with this tool:

- Drag the sliders until you can predict which way a statistic will move before it moves.
- For each test, find the point where the result crosses the significance threshold, then say out loud why.
- Practice naming your degrees of freedom every time you change a sample size.
- After each visualization, cover the result and write the APA sentence yourself, then check it.
- Spend the most time on Section 0. On the practice final, the single most common question is "which test is appropriate, be as specific as possible."
:::

# 0. Choosing the right test

More points on this final come from picking the correct test than from any single calculation. The questions usually end with "be as specific as possible," so a vague answer like "a t-test" or "ANOVA" will lose points. Name the full test, including between- vs within-subjects and one- vs two-way.

Work down from your outcome variable.

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
    A[What is your outcome measure?] --> B[Counts / categories]
    A --> C[A continuous score]

    B --> B1[One categorical variable<br/>vs a hypothesized distribution]
    B --> B2[Two categorical variables,<br/>testing for association]
    B1 --> B1a[Chi-square goodness of fit]
    B2 --> B2a[Chi-square test of independence]

    C --> D[Relationship between<br/>two continuous variables?]
    C --> E[Comparing means?]

    D --> D1[Describe strength and direction]
    D --> D2[Predict Y from X / fit a line]
    D1 --> D1a[Pearson correlation r]
    D2 --> D2a[Linear regression]

    E --> F[One group vs a<br/>known/hypothesized value]
    E --> G[Two conditions]
    E --> H[Three or more conditions,<br/>one factor]
    E --> I[Two factors]

    F --> F1{Population SD known?}
    F1 -->|Yes| F1a[z-test]
    F1 -->|No| F1b[One-sample t-test]

    G --> G1{Same subjects<br/>in both conditions?}
    G1 -->|Different subjects| G1a[Independent-samples t-test]
    G1 -->|Same subjects| G1b[Paired / related-samples t-test]

    H --> H1{Same subjects<br/>across conditions?}
    H1 -->|Different subjects| H1a[One-way between-subjects ANOVA]
    H1 -->|Same subjects| H1b[One-way within-subjects ANOVA]

    I --> I1[Two-way ANOVA<br/>two main effects + interaction]
```

::: {.callout-note title="Measurement scales (they show up every term)"}
The scale of your data decides what is even possible. Two mnemonics from the midterm review:

- **Order, Subtraction, Division, Zero**: "Orange Snakes Dunk Zebras." Ordinal adds order, interval allows subtraction (equal spacing), ratio allows division and has a true zero.
- **Nominal, Ordinal, Interval, Ratio**: "No Order Is Right."

Nominal and ordinal data are usually counts, which points you toward chi-square. Interval and ratio data are scores, which point you toward the mean-based tests and correlation/regression.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Null hypotheses, all in one place"}
| Test | Null hypothesis (H₀) |
|---|---|
| One-sample t / z | $\mu = \mu_0$ |
| Independent-samples t | $\mu_1 = \mu_2$ |
| Paired-samples t | $\mu_d = 0$ |
| One-way ANOVA | $\mu_1 = \mu_2 = \dots = \mu_k$ |
| Two-way ANOVA | No main effect of A; no main effect of B; no A×B interaction |
| Correlation | $\rho = 0$ |
| Linear regression | slope $\beta = 0$ |
| Chi-square | the variables are independent / observed frequencies match expected |
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="One-tailed or two-tailed?"}
The mean-based and relationship tests can be run one- or two-tailed: z-test, one-sample t, two-sample t, Pearson correlation, and linear regression. Chi-square is non-directional by construction, so it is not described as one- or two-tailed.
:::

# 1. Central Limit Theorem (CLT)

The **Central Limit Theorem** states that the sampling distribution of the sample mean approaches a Normal distribution as the sample size (n) grows — regardless of the shape of the underlying population distribution.

Key takeaways

- The **mean** of the sampling distribution equals the population mean (μ)
- The **spread** (standard error) shrinks as sample size *n* increases: SE = σ / √n
- Even highly skewed or bimodal populations produce approximately Normal sampling distributions with enough samples

The tendency for our samples to create this type of normal distribution is what enables most of our other statistical tests. 

**How to use this app:** Choose a population shape, set the sample size (*n*), then drag the "Number of samples" slider slowly from left to right to watch the sampling distribution build up. Try setting your sample size to 1, 10, and 100. Do you see much of a difference beyond that?

Notable milestones for a normally-distributed dataset: **1 sample** (almost nothing), **10 samples** (rough shape), **100 samples** (clearly bell-shaped), **300 samples** (well-converged).

However, note how the sample size changes how quickly the correct mean is estimated. 

```{shinylive-r}
#| viewerHeight: 550
#| standalone: true

library(shiny)

ui <- fluidPage(
  titlePanel("Central Limit Theorem"),
  sidebarLayout(
    sidebarPanel(
      selectInput("dist", "Population shape",
        choices = c("Normal" = "normal",
                    "Right-skewed" = "skewed",
                    "Uniform" = "uniform",
                    "Bimodal" = "bimodal")),
      sliderInput("n", "Sample size (n)", min = 1, max = 50, value = 5),
      sliderInput("n_sims", "Number of samples drawn", min = 1, max = 300, value = 1),
      hr(),
      helpText("Drag 'Number of samples' slowly to watch the sampling distribution build up.")
    ),
    mainPanel(
      plotOutput("cltPlot", height = "380px"),
      uiOutput("callout")
    )
  )
)

server <- function(input, output) {

  population <- reactive({
    set.seed(110)
    switch(input$dist,
      normal  = rnorm(50, mean = 21, sd = 1.5),
      skewed  = c(rnorm(40, mean = 19, sd = 1), rnorm(10, mean = 27, sd = 2)),
      uniform = runif(200, min = 18, max = 26),
      bimodal = c(rnorm(100, mean = 18, sd = 1), rnorm(100, mean = 24, sd = 1))
    )
  })

  sample_means <- reactive({
    set.seed(110)
    pop <- population()
    replicate(input$n_sims, mean(sample(pop, input$n, replace = TRUE)))
  })

  output$cltPlot <- renderPlot({
    pop   <- population()
    means <- sample_means()
    n_sims <- input$n_sims
    true_mean <- mean(pop)

    par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))

    # Panel 1: Population
    hist(pop,
         breaks = 20,
         col    = "skyblue",
         border = "white",
         main   = "Population Distribution",
         xlab   = "Value",
         xlim   = range(pop) + c(-1, 1))
    abline(v = true_mean, col = "red", lwd = 3)
    legend("topleft", legend = paste("μ =", round(true_mean, 2)),
           col = "red", lwd = 2, bty = "n", cex = 0.85)

    # Panel 2: Sampling distribution
    xlim_range <- range(c(means, pop)) + c(-1, 1)
    hist(means,
         breaks = max(5, min(30, n_sims %/% 5)),
         col    = "tomato",
         border = "white",
         main   = sprintf("Sampling Distribution\n(%d sample%s, n = %d)",
                          n_sims, if (n_sims == 1) "" else "s", input$n),
         xlab   = "Sample mean",
         xlim   = xlim_range)
    abline(v = true_mean,   col = "red",  lwd = 3)
    abline(v = mean(means), col = "blue", lwd = 3, lty = 2)
    legend("topleft",
           legend = c(paste("True μ =", round(true_mean, 2)),
                      paste("x̄ of means =", round(mean(means), 2))),
           col = c("red", "blue"), lwd = 2, lty = c(1, 2), bty = "n", cex = 0.85)
  })

  output$callout <- renderUI({
    means     <- sample_means()
    true_mean <- mean(population())
    n_sims    <- input$n_sims
    se_theory <- sd(population()) / sqrt(input$n)
    se_obs    <- sd(means)
    milestone <- if (n_sims == 1) {
      "Just 1 sample — almost no distribution to see yet."
    } else if (n_sims <= 10) {
      paste0("After ", n_sims, " samples: shape is very rough.")
    } else if (n_sims <= 100) {
      paste0("After ", n_sims, " samples: bell shape is emerging.")
    } else {
      paste0("After ", n_sims, " samples: well-converged to Normal.")
    }
    tags$div(
      style = "background:#f0f4f8; border-left:4px solid #2c7bb6; padding:10px 14px; margin-top:10px; border-radius:4px;",
      tags$b("Snapshot: "), milestone, tags$br(),
      sprintf("Running mean of sample means: %.3f (true μ = %.3f)", mean(means), true_mean), tags$br(),
      sprintf("Observed SE: %.3f | Theoretical SE (σ/√n): %.3f", se_obs, se_theory)
    )
  })
}

shinyApp(ui = ui, server = server)

```

# 2. Z-Test

A **z-test** is used when we know the **population standard deviation (σ)** — a rare but instructive scenario (e.g., when a large historical dataset gives us σ exactly).

$$z = \frac{\bar{x} - \mu_0}{\sigma / \sqrt{n}}$$

Because σ is known, we compare to the **Standard Normal** (not a *t*-distribution). The critical value is basically always ±1.96 for α = 0.05, two-tailed, regardless of *n*. This is directly in contrast to t-tests, where the critical values shrink as n incraeses. 

::: {.callout-important title="The Null Hypothesis"}
The population mean equals our hypothesized value:

$$H_0: \mu = \mu_0$$

where $\mu_0$ is the specific value we're testing against (e.g., a national average).
:::

**How to use this app:** Notice how the z-test and t-test give nearly identical results when *n* is large — the *t*-distribution approaches Normal.

```{shinylive-r}
#| viewerHeight: 480
#| standalone: true 

library(shiny)

ui <- fluidPage(
  titlePanel("Z-Test (Known σ)"),
  sidebarLayout(
    sidebarPanel(
      sliderInput("mu0",         "Hypothesized mean (μ₀)",  15, 25, 20, step = 0.5),
      sliderInput("sample_mean", "Observed sample mean (x̄)", 15, 25, 21, step = 0.5),
      sliderInput("sigma",       "Known population SD (σ)",  0.5, 8, 2,  step = 0.1),
      sliderInput("n",           "Sample size (n)",           5, 200, 30)
    ),
    mainPanel(
      plotOutput("zPlot", height = "300px"),
      uiOutput("zResults")
    )
  )
)

server <- function(input, output) {

  z_stat <- reactive({
    (input$sample_mean - input$mu0) / (input$sigma / sqrt(input$n))
  })

  p_val <- reactive({
    2 * pnorm(-abs(z_stat()))
  })

  output$zPlot <- renderPlot({
    z    <- z_stat()
    z_c  <- 1.96
    x    <- seq(-5, 5, length.out = 500)
    y    <- dnorm(x)

    par(mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))
    plot(x, y, type = "l", lwd = 2,
         main = "Standard Normal Distribution",
         xlab = "z", ylab = "Density")
    x_lo <- x[x <= -z_c]; x_hi <- x[x >= z_c]
    polygon(c(min(x_lo), x_lo, -z_c), c(0, dnorm(x_lo), 0),
            col = rgb(0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 0.3), border = NA)
    polygon(c(min(x_hi), x_hi, z_c), c(0, dnorm(x_hi), 0),
            col = rgb(0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 0.3), border = NA)
    abline(v =  z,   col = "navy",   lwd = 2.5, lty = 2)
    abline(v =  z_c, col = "tomato", lwd = 1.5, lty = 3)
    abline(v = -z_c, col = "tomato", lwd = 1.5, lty = 3)
    legend("topleft",
           legend = c(sprintf("z = %.3f", z),
                      "±z_crit = ±1.96",
                      "Rejection region (α=0.05)"),
           col = c("navy", "tomato", rgb(0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5)),
           lwd = c(2.5, 1.5, 8), lty = c(2, 3, 1), bty = "n", cex = 0.85)
  })

  output$zResults <- renderUI({
    z      <- z_stat()
    p      <- p_val()
    reject <- p < 0.05
    color  <- if (reject) "#c0392b" else "#27ae60"
    decision <- if (reject)
      sprintf("Reject H₀: μ₀ = %.1f (p < 0.05)", input$mu0)
    else
      sprintf("Fail to reject H₀: μ₀ = %.1f (p ≥ 0.05)", input$mu0)
    tags$div(
      style = paste0("background:#f9f9f9; border-left:4px solid ", color,
                     "; padding:10px 14px; margin-top:10px; border-radius:4px;"),
      tags$b("Results:"), tags$br(),
      sprintf("z = %.3f", z), tags$br(),
      sprintf("p-value = %.4f", p), tags$br(),
      tags$b(decision)
    )
  })
}

shinyApp(ui = ui, server = server)

```

# 3. One-Sample *t*-Test

A **one-sample *t*-test** asks: *Is our sample mean significantly different from a hypothesized population mean (μ₀)?* We often test against the hypothesis that our population mean is 0, and we test our sample after subtracting the sample mean from all observations. 

We use a *t*-statistic (not *z*) because **σ is unknown** and must be estimated from the sample:

$$t = \frac{\bar{x} - \mu_0}{s / \sqrt{n}}, \quad df = n - 1$$

The *p*-value is the probability of observing a *t*-statistic this extreme (or more) if H₀ were true.

::: {.callout-important title="The Null Hypothesis"}
The population mean equals our hypothesized value:

$$H_0: \mu = \mu_0$$

The only difference from the z-test is that we estimate $\sigma$ from our sample (as $s$) rather than knowing it.
:::

**How to use this app:** Adjust the sliders to see how moving μ₀ further from the observed mean, increasing *n*, or decreasing *s* all affect the *t*-statistic and *p*-value.

```{shinylive-r}
#| viewerHeight: 520
#| standalone: true

library(shiny)

ui <- fluidPage(
  titlePanel("One-Sample t-Test"),
  sidebarLayout(
    sidebarPanel(
      sliderInput("mu0",         "Hypothesized mean (μ₀)",  15, 25, 20, step = 0.5),
      sliderInput("sample_mean", "Observed sample mean (x̄)", 15, 25, 21, step = 0.5),
      sliderInput("sample_sd",   "Sample SD (s)",            0.5, 5, 2,  step = 0.1),
      sliderInput("n",           "Sample size (n)",           5, 100, 30)
    ),
    mainPanel(
      plotOutput("tPlot", height = "320px"),
      uiOutput("results")
    )
  )
)

server <- function(input, output) {

  stats <- reactive({
    t_stat <- (input$sample_mean - input$mu0) / (input$sample_sd / sqrt(input$n))
    df     <- input$n - 1
    p_val  <- 2 * pt(-abs(t_stat), df)
    list(t = t_stat, df = df, p = p_val)
  })

  output$tPlot <- renderPlot({
    s    <- stats()
    df   <- s$df
    t_ob <- s$t
    t_crit <- qt(0.975, df)
    x    <- seq(-5, 5, length.out = 500)
    y    <- dt(x, df)

    par(mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))
    plot(x, y, type = "l", lwd = 2,
         main = sprintf("t-Distribution (df = %d)", df),
         xlab = "t", ylab = "Density")

    # Shade rejection regions
    x_lo <- x[x <= -t_crit]; x_hi <- x[x >= t_crit]
    polygon(c(min(x_lo), x_lo, -t_crit), c(0, dt(x_lo, df), 0),
            col = rgb(0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 0.3), border = NA)
    polygon(c(min(x_hi), x_hi, t_crit), c(0, dt(x_hi, df), 0),
            col = rgb(0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 0.3), border = NA)

    abline(v = t_ob,    col = "navy",   lwd = 2.5, lty = 2)
    abline(v =  t_crit, col = "tomato", lwd = 1.5, lty = 3)
    abline(v = -t_crit, col = "tomato", lwd = 1.5, lty = 3)
    legend("topleft",
           legend = c(sprintf("t = %.3f", t_ob),
                      sprintf("±t_crit = ±%.3f", t_crit),
                      "Rejection region (α=0.05)"),
           col = c("navy", "tomato", rgb(0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5)),
           lwd = c(2.5, 1.5, 8), lty = c(2, 3, 1), bty = "n", cex = 0.85)
  })

  output$results <- renderUI({
    s      <- stats()
    reject <- s$p < 0.05
    color  <- if (reject) "#c0392b" else "#27ae60"
    decision <- if (reject)
      sprintf("Reject H₀: μ₀ = %.1f (p < 0.05)", input$mu0)
    else
      sprintf("Fail to reject H₀: μ₀ = %.1f (p ≥ 0.05)", input$mu0)

    tags$div(
      style = paste0("background:#f9f9f9; border-left:4px solid ", color,
                     "; padding:10px 14px; margin-top:10px; border-radius:4px;"),
      tags$b("Results:"), tags$br(),
      sprintf("t(%d) = %.3f", s$df, s$t), tags$br(),
      sprintf("p-value = %.4f", s$p), tags$br(),
      tags$b(decision)
    )
  })
}

shinyApp(ui = ui, server = server)

```

# 4. Two-Sample *t*-Test

A **two-sample *t*-test** tests whether the means of two groups differ:

$$H_0: \mu_1 = \mu_2$$

We can use either **independent** or **dependent** tests based on what our two groups represent. 

**When to use which:**

- **Independent samples t-test:** Different subjects in each group (e.g., treatment vs. control with separate participants)
- **Paired t-test:** Same subjects measured twice (e.g., pre-test vs. post-test, or same subject across two conditions)

## 4a. Independent samples

::: {.callout-important title="The Null Hypothesis"}
The two population means are equal:

$$H_0: \mu_1 = \mu_2$$

In other words, the difference between the means is zero: $\mu_1 - \mu_2 = 0$.
:::

Two variants:

- **Pooled (equal variances assumed):** combines variance estimates; uses *n₁ + n₂ − 2* df
- **Welch (unequal variances):** uses separate variance estimates with adjusted (Satterthwaite) df — generally safer, but not something you need to know for this course!. It might be instructive for you to see the difference between the two though, especially when setting the variances far apart from one another. The degrees of freedom for this version are adjusted. 

**CRITICAL: DON'T WORRY ABOUT THE WELCH TEST FOR ANYTHING OTHER THAN CURIOSITY**
(for now at least)

**How to use this app:** Slide Group 1 and Group 2 means apart to see when the test becomes significant. Toggle between pooled and Welch to compare. 

```{shinylive-r}
#| viewerHeight: 580
#| standalone: true

library(shiny)

ui <- fluidPage(
  titlePanel("Two-Sample t-Test"),
  sidebarLayout(
    sidebarPanel(
      tags$b("Group 1 (blue)"),
      sliderInput("mu1", "Mean₁",  10, 30, 20, step = 0.5),
      sliderInput("sd1", "SD₁",    0.5, 8,  2,  step = 0.5),
      sliderInput("n1",  "n₁",     5,  80,  30),
      tags$hr(),
      tags$b("Group 2 (red)"),
      sliderInput("mu2", "Mean₂",  10, 30, 22, step = 0.5),
      sliderInput("sd2", "SD₂",    0.5, 8,  2,  step = 0.5),
      sliderInput("n2",  "n₂",     5,  80,  30),
      tags$hr(),
      checkboxInput("equal_var", "Assume equal variances (pooled)", value = TRUE)
    ),
    mainPanel(
      plotOutput("twoSamplePlot", height = "380px"),
      uiOutput("twoResults")
    )
  )
)

server <- function(input, output) {

  samples <- reactive({
    set.seed(110)
    g1 <- rnorm(input$n1, input$mu1, input$sd1)
    g2 <- rnorm(input$n2, input$mu2, input$sd2)
    list(g1 = g1, g2 = g2)
  })

  test_result <- reactive({
    samp <- samples()
    t.test(samp$g1, samp$g2, var.equal = input$equal_var)
  })

  output$twoSamplePlot <- renderPlot({
    samp <- samples()
    res  <- test_result()
    t_ob <- res$statistic
    df   <- res$parameter
    t_crit <- qt(0.975, df)

    par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))

    # Panel 1: overlapping histograms
    all_vals <- c(samp$g1, samp$g2)
    xlim_h   <- range(all_vals) + c(-1, 1)
    hist(samp$g1, breaks = 15, col = rgb(0.18, 0.53, 0.78, 0.6),
         border = "white", xlim = xlim_h,
         main = "Sample Distributions", xlab = "Value")
    hist(samp$g2, breaks = 15, col = rgb(0.82, 0.24, 0.24, 0.6),
         border = "white", add = TRUE)
    abline(v = mean(samp$g1), col = "blue", lwd = 2, lty = 2)
    abline(v = mean(samp$g2), col = "red",  lwd = 2, lty = 2)
    legend("topleft",
           legend = c(sprintf("G1: x̄=%.1f", mean(samp$g1)),
                      sprintf("G2: x̄=%.1f", mean(samp$g2))),
           fill = c(rgb(0.18, 0.53, 0.78, 0.6), rgb(0.82, 0.24, 0.24, 0.6)),
           bty = "n", cex = 0.85)

    # Panel 2: t-distribution
    x <- seq(max(-8, -abs(t_ob) - 3), max(8, abs(t_ob) + 3), length.out = 500)
    y <- dt(x, df)
    plot(x, y, type = "l", lwd = 2,
         main = sprintf("t-Distribution (df = %.1f)", df),
         xlab = "t", ylab = "Density")
    x_lo <- x[x <= -t_crit]; x_hi <- x[x >= t_crit]
    if (length(x_lo) > 1)
      polygon(c(min(x_lo), x_lo, -t_crit), c(0, dt(x_lo, df), 0),
              col = rgb(0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 0.3), border = NA)
    if (length(x_hi) > 1)
      polygon(c(min(x_hi), x_hi, t_crit), c(0, dt(x_hi, df), 0),
              col = rgb(0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 0.3), border = NA)
    abline(v =  t_ob,   col = "navy",   lwd = 2.5, lty = 2)
    abline(v =  t_crit, col = "tomato", lwd = 1.5, lty = 3)
    abline(v = -t_crit, col = "tomato", lwd = 1.5, lty = 3)
  })

  output$twoResults <- renderUI({
    res    <- test_result()
    t_ob   <- res$statistic
    df     <- res$parameter
    p_val  <- res$p.value
    reject <- p_val < 0.05
    color  <- if (reject) "#c0392b" else "#27ae60"
    method <- if (input$equal_var) "Pooled (equal variances)" else "Welch (unequal variances)"
    decision <- if (reject) "Reject H₀: μ₁ = μ₂" else "Fail to reject H₀: μ₁ = μ₂"
    tags$div(
      style = paste0("background:#f9f9f9; border-left:4px solid ", color,
                     "; padding:10px 14px; margin-top:10px; border-radius:4px;"),
      tags$b("Results (", method, "):"), tags$br(),
      sprintf("t(%.1f) = %.3f", df, t_ob), tags$br(),
      sprintf("p-value = %.4f", p_val), tags$br(),
      tags$b(decision)
    )
  })
}

shinyApp(ui = ui, server = server)

```

## 4b. Paired Samples (Dependent t-Test)

A **paired t-test** is used when the same subjects are measured under two conditions (e.g., before/after treatment, left hand vs right hand, condition A vs condition B for the same person). 

::: {.callout-important title="The Null Hypothesis"}
There is no change in the mean when comparing the two observations:

$$H_0: \mu_d = 0$$

where $\mu_d$ is the mean of the difference scores (Condition 2 − Condition 1).
:::

Instead of comparing two independent groups, we compute the **difference score** for each subject and test whether the mean difference is significantly different from zero:

$$t = \frac{\bar{d} - \mu_0}{s_d / \sqrt{n}}, \quad df = n - 1$$

where $\bar{d}$ is the mean of the difference scores, $s_d$ is the SD of the differences, and $n$ is the **number of pairs** (not total observations).

::: {.callout-note title="The Key Insight"}
By using the **same subjects** in both conditions, we can subtract out individual differences. This is analogous to the relationship between the **between-groups ANOVA** and **within-groups (repeated measures) ANOVA** in Section 6 — using the same subjects across conditions removes between-subject variability from the error term, dramatically increasing statistical power.
:::

**How to use this app:** Adjust the between-subject SD and within-subject (error) SD to see how the paired test gains power. When between-subject variability is high but within-subject error is low, the paired test dramatically outperforms the independent test on the same data. Notice how small of a difference can be detected if you maximize the sample size and minimize within-subject error! 

```{shinylive-r}
#| viewerHeight: 620
#| standalone: true

library(shiny)

ui <- fluidPage(
  titlePanel("Paired t-Test"),
  sidebarLayout(
    sidebarPanel(
      sliderInput("n_pairs", "Number of subject pairs", 5, 50, 20),
      sliderInput("mu_diff", "True mean difference (Condition 2 - Condition 1)",
                  -5, 5, 1.5, step = 0.25),
      sliderInput("sd_subj", "Between-subject SD",
                  0.5, 8, 3, step = 0.5),
      sliderInput("sd_err",  "Within-subject error SD",
                  0.25, 5, 1, step = 0.25),
      tags$hr(),
      helpText("High between-subject SD + low error SD causes paired test to gain power vs. independent test.")
    ),
    mainPanel(
      plotOutput("pairedPlot", height = "400px"),
      uiOutput("pairedResults")
    )
  )
)

server <- function(input, output) {

  paired_data <- reactive({
    set.seed(110)
    n <- input$n_pairs
    subj_fx <- rnorm(n, 0, input$sd_subj)  # individual baseline
    c1 <- subj_fx + rnorm(n, 0, input$sd_err)
    c2 <- subj_fx + input$mu_diff + rnorm(n, 0, input$sd_err)
    data.frame(subject = 1:n, c1 = c1, c2 = c2, diff = c2 - c1)
  })

  paired_test <- reactive({
    d <- paired_data()
    t.test(d$c2, d$c1, paired = TRUE)
  })

  indep_test <- reactive({
    d <- paired_data()
    t.test(d$c2, d$c1, paired = FALSE, var.equal = TRUE)
  })

  output$pairedPlot <- renderPlot({
    d <- paired_data()
    res <- paired_test()
    t_ob <- res$statistic
    df   <- res$parameter
    t_crit <- qt(0.975, df)

    par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))

    # Panel 1: individual subject trajectories
    ylim_r <- range(c(d$c1, d$c2)) + c(-1, 1)
    plot(1:2, c(mean(d$c1), mean(d$c2)), type = "n",
         xlim = c(0.5, 2.5), ylim = ylim_r,
         xlab = "Condition", ylab = "Value",
         main = "Subject-level Differences",
         xaxt = "n")
    axis(1, at = 1:2, labels = c("C1", "C2"))

    for (i in 1:nrow(d)) {
      lines(1:2, c(d$c1[i], d$c2[i]), col = rgb(0, 0, 0.8, 0.3), lwd = 1)
      points(1:2, c(d$c1[i], d$c2[i]), col = rgb(0, 0, 0.8, 0.4), pch = 16, cex = 0.8)
    }
    lines(1:2, c(mean(d$c1), mean(d$c2)), col = "navy", lwd = 3)
    points(1:2, c(mean(d$c1), mean(d$c2)), col = "navy", pch = 19, cex = 1.6)

    # Panel 2: histogram of difference scores
    hist(d$diff, breaks = 12, col = "tomato", border = "white",
         main = "Distribution of Differences",
         xlab = "Difference (C2 - C1)")
    abline(v = 0, col = "gray40", lwd = 2, lty = 3)
    abline(v = mean(d$diff), col = "navy", lwd = 3, lty = 2)
    legend("topleft",
           legend = c("Zero (H₀)", sprintf("Mean diff = %.2f", mean(d$diff))),
           col = c("gray40", "navy"), lwd = 2, lty = c(3, 2), bty = "n", cex = 0.85)
  })

  output$pairedResults <- renderUI({
    res_p <- paired_test()
    res_i <- indep_test()
    t_p   <- res_p$statistic
    p_p   <- res_p$p.value
    t_i   <- res_i$statistic
    p_i   <- res_i$p.value
    reject <- p_p < 0.05
    color  <- if (reject) "#c0392b" else "#27ae60"
    decision <- if (reject) "Reject H₀: Mean difference ≠ 0"
                else "Fail to reject H₀: Mean difference = 0"

    tags$div(
      style = paste0("background:#f9f9f9; border-left:4px solid ", color,
                     "; padding:10px 14px; margin-top:10px; border-radius:4px;"),
      tags$b("Paired t-Test Results:"), tags$br(),
      sprintf("t(%.0f) = %.3f", res_p$parameter, t_p), tags$br(),
      sprintf("p-value = %.4f", p_p), tags$br(),
      tags$b(decision), tags$br(), tags$br(),
      tags$b("Compare to Independent Samples t-Test on same data:"), tags$br(),
      sprintf("t(%.0f) = %.3f, p = %.4f", res_i$parameter, t_i, p_i), tags$br(),
      tags$em("Notice how the paired test typically has a larger |t| and smaller p-value when between-subject variability is high.")
    )
  })
}

shinyApp(ui = ui, server = server)
```
# 5. Confidence Intervals & Effect Sizes

Hypothesis testing gives you a yes/no decision. **Estimation** asks a different question: what range of values is plausible for the parameter? A **confidence interval** sets an upper and lower limit that, across repeated samples, contains the population value a set percentage of the time.

$$\text{CI} = \bar{x} \pm t(s_{\bar{x}}), \quad s_{\bar{x}} = \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}$$

::: {.callout-note title="The link between a CI and a hypothesis test"}
A 95% confidence interval and a two-tailed test at α = 0.05 carry the same information. If the hypothesized value $\mu_0$ falls **outside** the interval, you would reject H₀. If it falls **inside**, you retain H₀. Watch the decision box flip as you slide $\mu_0$ across an interval edge.
:::

**Effect sizes** answer "how big," which significance alone never tells you. The sheet gives you three:

- **Cohen's d** $= \dfrac{\bar{x} - \mu_0}{s}$, in standard-deviation units (small 0.2, medium 0.5, large 0.8).
- **Proportion of variance** $r^2 = \dfrac{t^2}{t^2 + df}$ (item 11), the share of variability explained.
- **Omega-squared** $\omega^2 = \dfrac{t^2 - 1}{t^2 + df}$ (item 12), a more conservative version of the same idea.

**How to use this app:** Move $\mu_0$ toward and past the interval edge and watch the decision flip. Then change $n$ and $s$ to see the interval tighten or widen, and notice that Cohen's d does **not** depend on $n$ while the p-value does.

```{shinylive-r}
#| viewerHeight: 560
#| standalone: true

library(shiny)

ui <- fluidPage(
  titlePanel("Confidence Interval & Effect Size (one mean)"),
  sidebarLayout(
    sidebarPanel(
      sliderInput("xbar",  "Observed sample mean (x̄)", 15, 25, 21, step = 0.5),
      sliderInput("mu0",   "Hypothesized mean (μ₀)",   15, 25, 20, step = 0.5),
      sliderInput("s",     "Sample SD (s)",            0.5, 6, 2, step = 0.1),
      sliderInput("n",     "Sample size (n)",          5, 100, 30),
      selectInput("conf",  "Confidence level",
        choices = c("90%" = 0.90, "95%" = 0.95, "99%" = 0.99), selected = 0.95)
    ),
    mainPanel(
      plotOutput("ciPlot", height = "330px"),
      uiOutput("ciResults")
    )
  )
)

server <- function(input, output) {

  stats <- reactive({
    conf <- as.numeric(input$conf)
    df   <- input$n - 1
    se   <- input$s / sqrt(input$n)
    tcrit <- qt(1 - (1 - conf) / 2, df)
    lo   <- input$xbar - tcrit * se
    hi   <- input$xbar + tcrit * se
    t_stat <- (input$xbar - input$mu0) / se
    p_val  <- 2 * pt(-abs(t_stat), df)
    d      <- (input$xbar - input$mu0) / input$s
    r2     <- t_stat^2 / (t_stat^2 + df)
    w2     <- (t_stat^2 - 1) / (t_stat^2 + df)
    list(conf = conf, df = df, se = se, lo = lo, hi = hi,
         t = t_stat, p = p_val, d = d, r2 = r2, w2 = max(w2, 0))
  })

  output$ciPlot <- renderPlot({
    s <- stats()
    par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))

    # Panel 1: the interval on a number line
    inside <- (input$mu0 >= s$lo && input$mu0 <= s$hi)
    band   <- if (inside) rgb(0.15, 0.68, 0.38, 0.25) else rgb(0.75, 0.22, 0.17, 0.25)
    xr <- range(c(s$lo, s$hi, input$mu0)) + c(-1, 1)
    plot(NA, xlim = xr, ylim = c(0, 1), yaxt = "n", ylab = "",
         xlab = "Value", main = sprintf("%d%% Confidence Interval", round(s$conf * 100)))
    rect(s$lo, 0.35, s$hi, 0.65, col = band, border = NA)
    segments(s$lo, 0.5, s$hi, 0.5, lwd = 3, col = "gray30")
    segments(c(s$lo, s$hi), 0.4, c(s$lo, s$hi), 0.6, lwd = 3, col = "gray30")
    points(input$xbar, 0.5, pch = 19, cex = 1.8, col = "navy")
    abline(v = input$mu0, col = "tomato", lwd = 2.5, lty = 2)
    text(input$xbar, 0.78, sprintf("x̄ = %.2f", input$xbar), col = "navy", cex = 0.9)
    text(input$mu0, 0.22, sprintf("μ₀ = %.1f", input$mu0), col = "tomato", cex = 0.9)
    legend("topleft", legend = sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", s$lo, s$hi), bty = "n", cex = 0.9)

    # Panel 2: Cohen's d against conventional benchmarks
    dd <- s$d
    plot(NA, xlim = c(0, max(1, abs(dd) * 1.2)), ylim = c(0, 1), yaxt = "n", ylab = "",
         xlab = "|Cohen's d|", main = "Effect size (Cohen's d)")
    abline(v = c(0.2, 0.5, 0.8), col = "gray70", lty = 3)
    text(c(0.2, 0.5, 0.8), 0.95, c("small", "medium", "large"), col = "gray50", cex = 0.8)
    segments(0, 0.5, abs(dd), 0.5, lwd = 8, col = rgb(0.18, 0.53, 0.78, 0.7))
    points(abs(dd), 0.5, pch = 19, cex = 1.5, col = "navy")
    text(abs(dd), 0.3, sprintf("d = %.2f", dd), col = "navy", cex = 1)
  })

  output$ciResults <- renderUI({
    s <- stats()
    inside <- (input$mu0 >= s$lo && input$mu0 <= s$hi)
    color  <- if (inside) "#27ae60" else "#c0392b"
    decision <- if (inside)
      sprintf("μ₀ = %.1f is inside the interval: retain H₀ (consistent with p ≥ %.2f)",
              input$mu0, 1 - s$conf)
    else
      sprintf("μ₀ = %.1f is outside the interval: reject H₀ (consistent with p < %.2f)",
              input$mu0, 1 - s$conf)
    tags$div(
      style = paste0("background:#f9f9f9; border-left:4px solid ", color,
                     "; padding:10px 14px; margin-top:10px; border-radius:4px;"),
      tags$b(sprintf("%d%% CI: [%.2f, %.2f]", round(s$conf * 100), s$lo, s$hi)), tags$br(),
      sprintf("t(%d) = %.3f, p = %.4f", s$df, s$t, s$p), tags$br(),
      tags$b(decision), tags$br(), tags$br(),
      tags$b("Effect sizes: "),
      sprintf("Cohen's d = %.3f | r² = %.3f | ω² = %.3f", s$d, s$r2, s$w2), tags$br(),
      tags$em(sprintf("r² says about %.0f%% of the variability is explained.", 100 * s$r2))
    )
  })
}

shinyApp(ui = ui, server = server)
```

# 6. One-Way ANOVA

ANOVA (Analysis of Variance) tests whether **the variance of 2 or more group means** are equal. In practice, it's usually used for **3 or more groups**, but it's important to understand that you can use it for comparing two groups.

::: {.callout-tip title="Performing an ANOVA on only 2 groups"}
One-way ANOVA on two groups actually gives you the **same p-value as a pooled two-sample t-test!**

In other words, when performing an ANOVA for two groups:

$$F = t^2$$

Remember that this is **NOT** the case when there are 3 or more groups, which is the usual time you'll see ANOVA being used.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="The Null Hypothesis"}
There is no difference between any of the group means:

$$H_0: \mu_1 = \mu_2 = \mu_3 = \dots = \mu_k$$
:::

If you get a significant *p*-value on these tests, you often will follow up with a post-hoc test to identify which of the groups has the difference. 

It partitions total variance into:

- **Between-groups (SS_B):** variance due to group differences
- **Within-groups / Error (SS_W):** variance within groups

The **F-statistic** = MS_Between / MS_Within. Large F indicates that the **means differ more than chance**.

$$F = \frac{MS_{Between}}{MS_{Within}} = \frac{SS_B / (k-1)}{SS_W / (N-k)}$$

## 6a. Between-Groups ANOVA

Independent groups — different subjects in each condition. This is roughly analogous to the independent-sample *t*-test. You assume that there is no underlying structure or shared variance between your groups in this case. 

```{shinylive-r}
#| viewerHeight: 620
#| standalone: true

library(shiny)

ui <- fluidPage(
  titlePanel("Between-Groups One-Way ANOVA"),
  sidebarLayout(
    sidebarPanel(
      sliderInput("k", "Number of groups", 2, 5, 3),
      tags$b("Group means (μ):"),
      sliderInput("mu1g", "Group 1 mean", 10, 30, 20, step = 0.5),
      sliderInput("mu2g", "Group 2 mean", 10, 30, 22, step = 0.5),
      sliderInput("mu3g", "Group 3 mean", 10, 30, 24, step = 0.5),
      conditionalPanel("input.k >= 4",
        sliderInput("mu4g", "Group 4 mean", 10, 30, 26, step = 0.5)),
      conditionalPanel("input.k >= 5",
        sliderInput("mu5g", "Group 5 mean", 10, 30, 28, step = 0.5)),
      tags$hr(),
      sliderInput("sd_g",  "Within-group SD (all groups)", 0.5, 8, 3, step = 0.5),
      sliderInput("n_g",   "n per group",                   5,  40, 20)
    ),
    mainPanel(
      plotOutput("anovaPlot", height = "350px"),
      tableOutput("anovaTable"),
      uiOutput("anovaResult")
    )
  )
)

server <- function(input, output) {

  anova_data <- reactive({
    set.seed(110)
    k   <- input$k
    mus <- c(input$mu1g, input$mu2g, input$mu3g,
             if (k >= 4) input$mu4g else NULL,
             if (k >= 5) input$mu5g else NULL)[seq_len(k)]
    grp_list <- lapply(seq_len(k), function(i)
      data.frame(value = rnorm(input$n_g, mus[i], input$sd_g),
                 group = factor(paste0("G", i))))
    do.call(rbind, grp_list)
  })

  aov_result <- reactive({
    d <- anova_data()
    summary(aov(value ~ group, data = d))
  })

  output$anovaPlot <- renderPlot({
    d   <- anova_data()
    res <- aov_result()
    F_ob   <- res[[1]]$`F value`[1]
    df_bet <- res[[1]]$Df[1]
    df_wit <- res[[1]]$Df[2]
    F_crit <- qf(0.95, df_bet, df_wit)
    pal    <- c("skyblue", "tomato", "seagreen", "gold", "orchid")

    par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))

    # Panel 1: boxplot of groups
    boxplot(value ~ group, data = d,
            col    = pal[seq_len(input$k)],
            border = "gray30",
            main   = "Group Distributions",
            xlab   = "Group", ylab   = "Value")
    stripchart(value ~ group, data = d,
               method = "jitter", add = TRUE, pch = 16,
               col = rgb(0, 0, 0, 0.3), vertical = TRUE)

    # Panel 2: F-distribution
    x_max <- max(F_crit * 2.5, F_ob * 1.3, 6)
    x <- seq(0, x_max, length.out = 500)
    y <- df(x, df_bet, df_wit)
    plot(x, y, type = "l", lwd = 2,
         main = sprintf("F(%d, %d) Distribution", df_bet, df_wit),
         xlab = "F", ylab = "Density")
    x_rej <- x[x >= F_crit]
    if (length(x_rej) > 1)
      polygon(c(F_crit, x_rej, max(x_rej)), c(0, df(x_rej, df_bet, df_wit), 0),
              col = rgb(0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 0.3), border = NA)
    abline(v = F_ob,   col = "navy",   lwd = 2.5, lty = 2)
    abline(v = F_crit, col = "tomato", lwd = 1.5, lty = 3)
    legend("topleft",
           legend = c(sprintf("F = %.3f", F_ob),
                      sprintf("F_crit = %.3f", F_crit)),
           col = c("navy", "tomato"), lwd = 2, lty = c(2, 3), bty = "n", cex = 0.85)
  })

  output$anovaTable <- renderTable({
    res <- aov_result()
    tbl <- res[[1]]
    data.frame(
      Source    = c("Between Groups", "Within Groups (Error)"),
      SS        = round(tbl$`Sum Sq`, 3),
      df        = tbl$Df,
      MS        = round(tbl$`Mean Sq`, 3),
      F         = c(round(tbl$`F value`[1], 3), NA),
      p         = c(round(tbl$`Pr(>F)`[1], 4), NA),
      check.names = FALSE
    )
  }, na = "", striped = TRUE, bordered = TRUE, hover = TRUE)

  output$anovaResult <- renderUI({
    res    <- aov_result()
    p_val  <- res[[1]]$`Pr(>F)`[1]
    reject <- p_val < 0.05
    color  <- if (reject) "#c0392b" else "#27ae60"
    decision <- if (reject) "Reject H₀: At least one group mean differs (p < 0.05)"
                else "Fail to reject H₀: No significant difference between group means (p ≥ 0.05)"
    tags$div(
      style = paste0("background:#f9f9f9; border-left:4px solid ", color,
                     "; padding:8px 14px; border-radius:4px;"),
      tags$b(decision)
    )
  })
}

shinyApp(ui = ui, server = server)

```

---

## 6b. Within-Groups (Repeated Measures) ANOVA

::: {.callout-important title="The Null Hypothesis"}
There is no change in the group mean across all observations:

$$H_0: \mu_1 = \mu_2 = \dots = \mu_k$$

where each $\mu_i$ represents the mean for the same subjects measured under condition $i$.
:::

The same subjects are measured across all conditions. Subject-to-subject variability is **removed** from the error term, dramatically increasing statistical power.

$$F_{RM} = \frac{MS_{Conditions}}{MS_{Conditions \times Subjects}}$$

The line plot below shows individual "subjects" across conditions. Parallel lines are good and indicate low within-subject error. This results in a high *F*.

REMEMBER: While t-scores are universally accepted as having clearly delineated conventional effect thresholds (d = 0.2 | 0.5 | 0.8), **F tests do not have common effect sizes**. Depending on your dataset, explaining 25% of the variance could be excellent! However, if you're looking at a cancer screening test, it is likely far too low.  

```{shinylive-r}
#| viewerHeight: 620
#| standalone: true

library(shiny)

ui <- fluidPage(
  titlePanel("Within-Groups (Repeated Measures) ANOVA"),
  sidebarLayout(
    sidebarPanel(
      sliderInput("k_rm",   "Number of conditions",    2, 4,   3),
      sliderInput("n_subj", "Number of subjects",      5, 40,  20),
      sliderInput("mu_diff","Mean difference across conditions", 0, 8, 2, step = 0.5),
      sliderInput("sd_subj","Between-subject SD",      0.5, 8, 3, step = 0.5),
      sliderInput("sd_err", "Within-subject error SD", 0.5, 5, 1, step = 0.25),
      helpText("High between-subject SD + low error SD = RM ANOVA gains the most power.")
    ),
    mainPanel(
      plotOutput("rmPlot", height = "380px"),
      tableOutput("rmTable"),
      uiOutput("rmResult")
    )
  )
)

server <- function(input, output) {

  rm_data <- reactive({
    set.seed(110)
    k       <- input$k_rm
    n       <- input$n_subj
    subj_fx <- rnorm(n, 0, input$sd_subj)  # random subject intercepts
    cond_fx <- seq(0, input$mu_diff, length.out = k)

    rows <- expand.grid(subject = 1:n, condition = 1:k)
    rows$value <- subj_fx[rows$subject] + cond_fx[rows$condition] +
                  rnorm(nrow(rows), 0, input$sd_err)
    rows$subject   <- factor(rows$subject)
    rows$condition <- factor(rows$condition,
                             labels = paste0("C", seq_len(k)))
    rows
  })

  rm_aov <- reactive({
    d <- rm_data()
    summary(aov(value ~ condition + Error(subject/condition), data = d))
  })

  output$rmPlot <- renderPlot({
    d   <- rm_data()
    res <- rm_aov()

    # Extract F from within-subject stratum
    within_tbl <- res[["Error: subject:condition"]][[1]]
    F_ob   <- within_tbl$`F value`[1]
    df_cond <- within_tbl$Df[1]
    df_err  <- within_tbl$Df[2]
    F_crit  <- qf(0.95, df_cond, df_err)

    par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))

    # Panel 1: individual trajectories
    conds   <- levels(d$condition)
    n_conds <- length(conds)
    cond_means <- tapply(d$value, d$condition, mean)
    ylim_r  <- range(d$value) + c(-0.5, 0.5)

    plot(1:n_conds, cond_means, type = "n",
         xlim = c(0.5, n_conds + 0.5), ylim = ylim_r,
         xlab = "Condition", ylab = "Value",
         main = "Individual Subject Trajectories",
         xaxt = "n")
    axis(1, at = 1:n_conds, labels = conds)

    for (subj in levels(d$subject)) {
      vals <- d$value[d$subject == subj]
      lines(1:n_conds, vals, col = rgb(0, 0, 0.8, 0.25), lwd = 1)
    }
    lines(1:n_conds, cond_means, col = "navy", lwd = 3)
    points(1:n_conds, cond_means, col = "navy", pch = 19, cex = 1.4)

    # Panel 2: F distribution
    x_max <- max(F_crit * 2.5, F_ob * 1.3, 6)
    x <- seq(0, x_max, length.out = 500)
    y <- df(x, df_cond, df_err)
    plot(x, y, type = "l", lwd = 2,
         main = sprintf("F(%d, %d) Distribution", df_cond, df_err),
         xlab = "F", ylab = "Density")
    x_rej <- x[x >= F_crit]
    if (length(x_rej) > 1)
      polygon(c(F_crit, x_rej, max(x_rej)), c(0, df(x_rej, df_cond, df_err), 0),
              col = rgb(0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 0.3), border = NA)
    abline(v = F_ob,   col = "navy",   lwd = 2.5, lty = 2)
    abline(v = F_crit, col = "tomato", lwd = 1.5, lty = 3)
    legend("topleft",
           legend = c(sprintf("F = %.3f", F_ob),
                      sprintf("F_crit = %.3f", F_crit)),
           col = c("navy", "tomato"), lwd = 2, lty = c(2, 3), bty = "n", cex = 0.85)
  })

  output$rmTable <- renderTable({
    res <- rm_aov()
    within_tbl <- res[["Error: subject:condition"]][[1]]
    data.frame(
      Source = c("Conditions (Between)", "Error (Conditions × Subjects)"),
      SS     = round(within_tbl$`Sum Sq`, 3),
      df     = within_tbl$Df,
      MS     = round(within_tbl$`Mean Sq`, 3),
      F      = c(round(within_tbl$`F value`[1], 3), NA),
      p      = c(round(within_tbl$`Pr(>F)`[1], 4), NA),
      check.names = FALSE
    )
  }, na = "", striped = TRUE, bordered = TRUE, hover = TRUE)

  output$rmResult <- renderUI({
    res        <- rm_aov()
    within_tbl <- res[["Error: subject:condition"]][[1]]
    p_val      <- within_tbl$`Pr(>F)`[1]
    reject     <- p_val < 0.05
    color      <- if (reject) "#c0392b" else "#27ae60"
    decision   <- if (reject)
      "Reject H₀: Condition means differ significantly (p < 0.05)"
    else
      "Fail to reject H₀: No significant effect of condition (p ≥ 0.05)"
    tags$div(
      style = paste0("background:#f9f9f9; border-left:4px solid ", color,
                     "; padding:8px 14px; border-radius:4px;"),
      tags$b(decision)
    )
  })
}

shinyApp(ui = ui, server = server)

```
# 7. Two-Way ANOVA

A **two-way between-subjects ANOVA** has two factors (call them A and B), with different subjects in every cell. Instead of one question it asks three, so it runs three hypothesis tests:

- **Main effect of A:** averaging over B, do the levels of A differ?
- **Main effect of B:** averaging over A, do the levels of B differ?
- **Interaction (A × B):** does the effect of A depend on the level of B?

::: {.callout-important title="Reading the interaction plot"}
Plot the cell means with one line per level of B.

- **Parallel lines** mean no interaction. The gap between lines is the same at every level of A.
- **Lines that converge, cross, or fan out** signal an interaction. The effect of one factor changes depending on the other.

When the interaction is significant, interpret it **first**, using simple main effects, before reading the main effects on their own.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Naming the parts (a common fill-in question)"}
For a design like "type of media exposure (violent, non-violent, none) and age group (early vs late adolescent) on aggression scores":

- **Dependent variable:** aggression scores (the measured outcome).
- **Factor A:** media exposure, with **3 levels**.
- **Factor B:** age group, with **2 levels**.

This is a 3 × 2 design. The app below uses a 2 × 2 so the interaction plot stays readable.
:::

**How to use this app:** Set the four cell means to make the two lines parallel and watch the interaction F drop toward nonsignificance. Then drag one corner to cross the lines and watch the interaction F climb.

```{shinylive-r}
#| viewerHeight: 640
#| standalone: true

library(shiny)

ui <- fluidPage(
  titlePanel("Two-Way Between-Subjects ANOVA (2 × 2)"),
  sidebarLayout(
    sidebarPanel(
      tags$b("Cell means"),
      sliderInput("m11", "A1 / B1", 10, 30, 18, step = 0.5),
      sliderInput("m12", "A1 / B2", 10, 30, 20, step = 0.5),
      sliderInput("m21", "A2 / B1", 10, 30, 22, step = 0.5),
      sliderInput("m22", "A2 / B2", 10, 30, 24, step = 0.5),
      tags$hr(),
      sliderInput("sd_w", "Within-cell SD", 0.5, 8, 3, step = 0.5),
      sliderInput("n_c",  "n per cell",      5, 40, 15)
    ),
    mainPanel(
      plotOutput("twoPlot", height = "320px"),
      tableOutput("twoTable"),
      uiOutput("twoResult")
    )
  )
)

server <- function(input, output) {

  dat <- reactive({
    set.seed(110)
    n <- input$n_c
    mk <- function(mu) rnorm(n, mu, input$sd_w)
    data.frame(
      value = c(mk(input$m11), mk(input$m12), mk(input$m21), mk(input$m22)),
      A = factor(rep(c("A1", "A1", "A2", "A2"), each = n)),
      B = factor(rep(c("B1", "B2", "B1", "B2"), each = n))
    )
  })

  fit <- reactive({
    tab <- summary(aov(value ~ A * B, data = dat()))[[1]]
    ss  <- tab[["Sum Sq"]]
    list(tab = tab, ss = ss, ss_tot = sum(ss))
  })

  output$twoPlot <- renderPlot({
    d  <- dat()
    cm <- tapply(d$value, list(d$A, d$B), mean)   # rows A1,A2 ; cols B1,B2
    par(mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))
    yr <- range(cm) + c(-2, 2)
    plot(NA, xlim = c(0.7, 2.3), ylim = yr, xaxt = "n",
         xlab = "Factor A", ylab = "Cell mean",
         main = "Interaction plot (one line per level of B)")
    axis(1, at = 1:2, labels = c("A1", "A2"))
    lines(1:2, cm[, "B1"], col = "navy",   lwd = 3, type = "b", pch = 19, cex = 1.5)
    lines(1:2, cm[, "B2"], col = "tomato", lwd = 3, type = "b", pch = 17, cex = 1.5)
    legend("topleft", legend = c("B1", "B2"),
           col = c("navy", "tomato"), lwd = 3, pch = c(19, 17), bty = "n", cex = 0.9)
  })

  output$twoTable <- renderTable({
    f   <- fit()
    tab <- f$tab
    eta <- f$ss / f$ss_tot
    data.frame(
      Source = c("Factor A", "Factor B", "A × B", "Error"),
      SS     = round(f$ss, 2),
      df     = tab[["Df"]],
      MS     = round(tab[["Mean Sq"]], 2),
      F      = c(round(tab[["F value"]][1:3], 3), NA),
      p      = c(round(tab[["Pr(>F)"]][1:3], 4), NA),
      "eta sq" = c(round(eta[1:3], 3), NA),
      check.names = FALSE
    )
  }, na = "", striped = TRUE, bordered = TRUE, hover = TRUE)

  output$twoResult <- renderUI({
    tab <- fit()$tab
    p   <- tab[["Pr(>F)"]]
    sig <- function(x) if (!is.na(x) && x < 0.05) "significant" else "not significant"
    tags$div(
      style = "background:#f9f9f9; border-left:4px solid #2c7bb6; padding:10px 14px; border-radius:4px;",
      tags$b("Decisions (α = 0.05):"), tags$br(),
      sprintf("Main effect A: %s (p = %.4f)", sig(p[1]), p[1]), tags$br(),
      sprintf("Main effect B: %s (p = %.4f)", sig(p[2]), p[2]), tags$br(),
      sprintf("A × B interaction: %s (p = %.4f)", sig(p[3]), p[3]), tags$br(),
      tags$em("If the interaction is significant, interpret it before the main effects.")
    )
  })
}

shinyApp(ui = ui, server = server)
```

# 8. Correlation (Pearson's r)

**Correlation** describes the strength and direction of the linear relationship between two continuous variables. Pearson's *r* runs from −1 to +1: the sign is the direction, and the distance from 0 is the strength.

$$r = \frac{SS_{XY}}{\sqrt{SS_X \, SS_Y}}, \qquad r^2 = \text{proportion of variance shared}$$

On the exam you may be handed the sums of squares and asked for *r* and the effect size. With $SS_{XY}$ and the product $SS_X \cdot SS_Y$ in hand, *r* is one division and a square root, and $r^2$ is just *r* squared (item 25, then the coefficient of determination).

::: {.callout-important title="Significance depends on n, not just the size of r"}
A given *r* is significant only if it beats the **critical value** for your degrees of freedom ($df = n - 2$). With small samples even a fairly large *r* can fail to reach significance. For example, $r = .26$ with $n = 40$ does **not** clear the two-tailed .05 cutoff. Watch the critical value in the results box as you change *n*.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="What correlation cannot do"}
- **Causation.** A relationship does not tell you which variable drives which, or whether a third variable drives both.
- **Outliers.** A single off-trend point can inflate or hide a correlation. Use the toggle below to see it.
- **Non-linearity.** *r* only measures the straight-line part of a relationship. A strong curved pattern can still give *r* near 0.
- **Restricted range** narrows the spread of scores and shrinks *r*.
:::

**How to use this app:** Set the underlying relationship strength and sample size, then read the observed *r*, its *r²*, and whether it clears the critical value. Flip on the outlier to see how much one point can move the result.

```{shinylive-r}
#| viewerHeight: 560
#| standalone: true

library(shiny)

ui <- fluidPage(
  titlePanel("Pearson Correlation"),
  sidebarLayout(
    sidebarPanel(
      sliderInput("rho", "Underlying relationship strength (population r)",
                  -0.95, 0.95, 0.5, step = 0.05),
      sliderInput("n",   "Sample size (n)", 5, 150, 40),
      checkboxInput("outlier", "Add one off-trend outlier", value = FALSE),
      helpText("df = n − 2. The critical value is the bar a correlation must clear to be significant.")
    ),
    mainPanel(
      plotOutput("scatter", height = "330px"),
      uiOutput("corResults")
    )
  )
)

server <- function(input, output) {

  dat <- reactive({
    set.seed(110)
    n   <- input$n
    rho <- input$rho
    x <- rnorm(n)
    y <- rho * x + sqrt(1 - rho^2) * rnorm(n)
    x <- 50 + 10 * x
    y <- 50 + 10 * y
    if (input$outlier) {
      x <- c(x, max(x) + 15)
      y <- c(y, min(y) - 15)
    }
    data.frame(x = x, y = y)
  })

  ct <- reactive({
    d <- dat()
    cor.test(d$x, d$y)
  })

  output$scatter <- renderPlot({
    d <- dat()
    r <- unname(ct()$estimate)
    par(mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))
    plot(d$x, d$y, pch = 19, col = rgb(0.18, 0.53, 0.78, 0.6),
         xlab = "X", ylab = "Y",
         main = sprintf("Scatter plot (r = %.3f)", r))
    fit <- lm(y ~ x, data = d)
    abline(fit, col = "navy", lwd = 2)
    if (input$outlier)
      points(d$x[nrow(d)], d$y[nrow(d)], pch = 1, cex = 3, lwd = 2, col = "tomato")
  })

  output$corResults <- renderUI({
    d   <- dat()
    res <- ct()
    r   <- unname(res$estimate)
    df  <- unname(res$parameter)
    p   <- res$p.value
    tcrit <- qt(0.975, df)
    rcrit <- tcrit / sqrt(df + tcrit^2)
    reject <- p < 0.05
    color  <- if (reject) "#c0392b" else "#27ae60"
    decision <- if (reject)
      sprintf("Significant: |r| = %.3f exceeds the critical r of %.3f", abs(r), rcrit)
    else
      sprintf("Not significant: |r| = %.3f does not reach the critical r of %.3f", abs(r), rcrit)
    tags$div(
      style = paste0("background:#f9f9f9; border-left:4px solid ", color,
                     "; padding:10px 14px; margin-top:10px; border-radius:4px;"),
      tags$b(sprintf("r = %.3f, r² = %.3f", r, r^2)), tags$br(),
      sprintf("t(%d) = %.3f, p = %.4f", df, unname(res$statistic), p), tags$br(),
      sprintf("Critical r (two-tailed, α = .05, df = %d): ±%.3f", df, rcrit), tags$br(),
      tags$b(decision), tags$br(),
      tags$em(sprintf("r² means about %.0f%% of the variance in one variable is shared with the other.",
                      100 * r^2))
    )
  })
}

shinyApp(ui = ui, server = server)
```

# 9. Linear Regression

Correlation describes a relationship; **linear regression** fits an equation to it so you can predict one variable from another.

$$\hat{Y} = bX + a$$

The **predictor** X is the known variable; the **criterion** Y is the one you predict. The slope *b* is the change in Y for a one-unit change in X (item 27). The intercept *a* is the predicted Y when X = 0. The line is chosen by **least squares**, the line that makes the squared vertical distances from the points (the **residuals**) as small as possible.

::: {.callout-note title="Residuals and homoscedasticity"}
A **residual** is the gap between an observed point and the line: observed minus predicted. Plotting residuals against X is how you check the regression's assumptions.

- **Homoscedastic:** residuals show roughly even spread across X. This is what you want.
- **Heteroscedastic:** the spread fans out or narrows across X. The line still fits, but the model's error is not constant, which violates an assumption.

Use the toggle to switch between the two and watch the residual plot.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Prediction is just plugging in"}
To predict, substitute an X into the fitted equation. For $\hat{Y} = -0.13X + 1.72$, a patient who attends 6 sessions has a predicted score of $-0.13(6) + 1.72 = 0.94$. You will not fit a regression by hand on this exam, but you are expected to read off the slope and intercept and predict from them.
:::

**How to use this app:** Set a slope and intercept, then move the prediction slider to read a predicted Y off the line. Turn on heteroscedasticity and watch the residual plot fan out while the line itself barely moves.

```{shinylive-r}
#| viewerHeight: 580
#| standalone: true

library(shiny)

ui <- fluidPage(
  titlePanel("Linear Regression"),
  sidebarLayout(
    sidebarPanel(
      sliderInput("b",  "Slope (b)",            -3, 3, 1.2, step = 0.1),
      sliderInput("a",  "Intercept (a)",        -5, 20, 5, step = 0.5),
      sliderInput("noise", "Residual spread",    0.5, 12, 4, step = 0.5),
      sliderInput("n",  "Sample size (n)",       10, 150, 50),
      sliderInput("xpred", "Predict Y at X =",   0, 20, 10, step = 0.5),
      checkboxInput("hetero", "Make residuals heteroscedastic", value = FALSE)
    ),
    mainPanel(
      plotOutput("regPlot", height = "340px"),
      uiOutput("regResults")
    )
  )
)

server <- function(input, output) {

  dat <- reactive({
    set.seed(110)
    n <- input$n
    x <- runif(n, 0, 20)
    sd_i <- if (input$hetero) input$noise * (0.25 + 1.5 * (x / 20)) else rep(input$noise, n)
    y <- input$a + input$b * x + rnorm(n, 0, sd_i)
    data.frame(x = x, y = y)
  })

  fit <- reactive(lm(y ~ x, data = dat()))

  output$regPlot <- renderPlot({
    d   <- dat()
    f   <- fit()
    co  <- coef(f)
    par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))

    # Panel 1: scatter + least-squares line + prediction
    plot(d$x, d$y, pch = 19, col = rgb(0.18, 0.53, 0.78, 0.55),
         xlab = "X (predictor)", ylab = "Y (criterion)",
         main = "Least-squares fit")
    abline(f, col = "navy", lwd = 2.5)
    ypred <- co[1] + co[2] * input$xpred
    segments(input$xpred, min(d$y) - 5, input$xpred, ypred, col = "tomato", lty = 2, lwd = 2)
    segments(min(d$x) - 5, ypred, input$xpred, ypred, col = "tomato", lty = 2, lwd = 2)
    points(input$xpred, ypred, pch = 19, col = "tomato", cex = 1.6)

    # Panel 2: residual plot
    res <- resid(f)
    plot(d$x, res, pch = 19, col = rgb(0.4, 0.4, 0.4, 0.6),
         xlab = "X", ylab = "Residual (observed − predicted)",
         main = "Residual plot")
    abline(h = 0, col = "navy", lwd = 2, lty = 1)
  })

  output$regResults <- renderUI({
    f  <- fit()
    co <- coef(f)
    r2 <- summary(f)$r.squared
    ypred <- co[1] + co[2] * input$xpred
    spread_note <- if (input$hetero)
      "Residuals fan out across X: heteroscedastic (assumption violated)."
    else
      "Residuals are evenly spread across X: homoscedastic (assumption met)."
    tags$div(
      style = "background:#f9f9f9; border-left:4px solid #2c7bb6; padding:10px 14px; margin-top:10px; border-radius:4px;",
      tags$b(sprintf("Fitted equation: Ŷ = %.3f·X + %.3f", co[2], co[1])), tags$br(),
      sprintf("r² = %.3f  (about %.0f%% of the variance in Y is explained by X)", r2, 100 * r2), tags$br(),
      sprintf("Predicted Y at X = %.1f:  Ŷ = %.2f", input$xpred, ypred), tags$br(),
      tags$em(spread_note)
    )
  })
}

shinyApp(ui = ui, server = server)
```

# 10. Chi-Square

Chi-square is for **counts in categories**, not means. It compares the frequencies you observed against the frequencies you would expect. There are two versions, and the exam wants you to name which one.

$$f_e = \frac{\text{row total} \times \text{column total}}{N}, \qquad \chi^2 = \sum \frac{(f_o - f_e)^2}{f_e}$$

- **Goodness of fit:** one categorical variable against a hypothesized distribution. $df = k - 1$, where *k* is the number of categories.
- **Test of independence:** two categorical variables, testing whether they are associated. $df = (\text{rows} - 1)(\text{columns} - 1)$.

::: {.callout-important title="Assumptions, including the soft one"}
- Each observation falls in **one and only one** category.
- Observations are **independent** (different, unrelated participants). Splitting one person's count across two categories breaks this.
- The **soft** assumption that researchers sometimes bend: every **expected** frequency should be at least **5**. The app warns you when this is violated.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Effect size"}
For a 2 × 2 table, the **phi coefficient** $\varphi = \sqrt{\chi^2 / N}$ (item 30). For larger tables, **Cramér's V** $= \sqrt{\chi^2 / (N \cdot df_{smaller})}$ (item 31), where $df_{smaller}$ is the smaller of (rows − 1) and (columns − 1). For a 2 × 2 the two are identical.
:::

**How to use this app:** Switch between the two tests. In goodness-of-fit, push one category's count far from the others and watch χ² grow. In the independence test, make the rows proportional to each other (no association) and watch χ² fall toward 0.

```{shinylive-r}
#| viewerHeight: 620
#| standalone: true

library(shiny)

ui <- fluidPage(
  titlePanel("Chi-Square: Goodness of Fit and Independence"),
  sidebarLayout(
    sidebarPanel(
      selectInput("mode", "Which test?",
        choices = c("Goodness of fit" = "gof", "Test of independence" = "ind")),
      conditionalPanel("input.mode == 'gof'",
        tags$b("Observed counts (4 categories)"),
        sliderInput("o1", "Category 1", 0, 60, 10),
        sliderInput("o2", "Category 2", 0, 60, 14),
        sliderInput("o3", "Category 3", 0, 60, 20),
        sliderInput("o4", "Category 4", 0, 60, 16),
        helpText("Expected = equal split of the total across the 4 categories.")
      ),
      conditionalPanel("input.mode == 'ind'",
        tags$b("Observed 2 × 2 table"),
        sliderInput("c11", "Row 1, Col 1", 0, 100, 40),
        sliderInput("c12", "Row 1, Col 2", 0, 100, 20),
        sliderInput("c21", "Row 2, Col 1", 0, 100, 20),
        sliderInput("c22", "Row 2, Col 2", 0, 100, 40)
      )
    ),
    mainPanel(
      plotOutput("chiPlot", height = "320px"),
      tableOutput("expTable"),
      uiOutput("chiResults")
    )
  )
)

server <- function(input, output) {

  analysis <- reactive({
    if (input$mode == "gof") {
      obs <- c(input$o1, input$o2, input$o3, input$o4)
      test <- chisq.test(obs)
      list(mode = "gof", obs = obs, exp = test$expected,
           stat = unname(test$statistic), df = unname(test$parameter),
           p = test$p.value, N = sum(obs))
    } else {
      m <- matrix(c(input$c11, input$c12, input$c21, input$c22),
                  nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)
      test <- chisq.test(m, correct = FALSE)
      list(mode = "ind", obs = m, exp = test$expected,
           stat = unname(test$statistic), df = unname(test$parameter),
           p = test$p.value, N = sum(m))
    }
  })

  output$chiPlot <- renderPlot({
    a <- analysis()
    par(mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))
    if (a$mode == "gof") {
      mat <- rbind(Observed = a$obs, Expected = a$exp)
      barplot(mat, beside = TRUE, col = c("navy", "gray70"), border = "white",
              names.arg = paste0("C", 1:4),
              main = "Observed vs Expected", ylab = "Frequency")
      legend("topright", legend = c("Observed", "Expected"),
             fill = c("navy", "gray70"), bty = "n")
    } else {
      barplot(a$obs, beside = TRUE, col = c("navy", "tomato"), border = "white",
              names.arg = c("Col 1", "Col 2"),
              main = "Observed counts by row", ylab = "Frequency")
      legend("topright", legend = c("Row 1", "Row 2"),
             fill = c("navy", "tomato"), bty = "n")
    }
  })

  output$expTable <- renderTable({
    a <- analysis()
    if (a$mode == "gof") {
      data.frame(Category = paste0("C", 1:4),
                 Observed = a$obs, Expected = round(a$exp, 2),
                 check.names = FALSE)
    } else {
      e <- round(a$exp, 2)
      data.frame(Row = c("Row 1", "Row 2"),
                 "Col 1 (exp)" = e[, 1], "Col 2 (exp)" = e[, 2],
                 check.names = FALSE)
    }
  }, striped = TRUE, bordered = TRUE)

  output$chiResults <- renderUI({
    a <- analysis()
    reject <- a$p < 0.05
    color  <- if (reject) "#c0392b" else "#27ae60"
    rows <- nrow(as.matrix(a$exp)); cols <- ncol(as.matrix(a$exp))
    df_small <- if (a$mode == "ind") min(rows - 1, cols - 1) else 1
    eff <- sqrt(a$stat / (a$N * df_small))
    eff_name <- if (a$mode == "ind" && rows == 2 && cols == 2) "φ (phi)" else
                if (a$mode == "ind") "Cramér's V" else NA
    decision <- if (reject) "Reject H₀: the frequencies differ from expected / the variables are associated."
                else "Retain H₀: no significant departure from expected."
    warn <- if (min(a$exp) < 5)
      tags$div(style = "color:#c0392b;", "Warning: an expected frequency is below 5 (assumption violated).")
    else NULL
    tags$div(
      style = paste0("background:#f9f9f9; border-left:4px solid ", color,
                     "; padding:10px 14px; margin-top:10px; border-radius:4px;"),
      tags$b(sprintf("χ²(%d) = %.3f, p = %.4f", a$df, a$stat, a$p)), tags$br(),
      if (a$mode == "ind") tags$span(sprintf("Effect size %s = %.3f", eff_name, eff)) else
        tags$span(sprintf("Total N = %d, k = 4 categories", a$N)),
      tags$br(),
      tags$b(decision),
      warn
    )
  })
}

shinyApp(ui = ui, server = server)
```
